report.source_text: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the abdomen was pursued to further investigate the double duct sign, which did not reveal choledocholithiasis or pancreaticobiliary malignancy. The dilated biliary tree was suspected to be secondary to thickened descending duodenum. This thickening was abutting the hepatic flexure. Additional findings included hydroureteronephrosis on the right with a focally enhancing soft tissue mass (Fig. 3).

report.source_text: Colonoscopy demonstrated a mass at the hepatic flexure (Fig. 5). Biopsies confirmed invasive transitional cell cancer.

clinician.final_diagnosis: gastric outlet obstruction due to duodenal wall circumferential thickening with adjacent inflammatory stranding from transitional cell carcinoma metastasis
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 73-year-old male with a history of stage IV transitional cell cancer presented with 5 weeks of nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. A CT scan revealed new circumferential thickening and inflammatory stranding at the descending/transverse duodenal junction and hepatic flexure, along with a double duct sign. Upper endoscopy showed duodenal stenosis, but biopsies were non-diagnostic. MRI further investigated the double duct sign, ruling out choledocholithiasis or pancreaticobiliary malignancy, and attributed the biliary dilation to the thickened descending duodenum, which was abutting the hepatic flexure. A subsequent colonoscopy identified a mass at the hepatic flexure, and biopsies confirmed invasive transitional cell cancer, thereby establishing the metastatic origin of the duodenal thickening causing gastric outlet obstruction.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Patient presented with symptoms consistent with gastric outlet obstruction: nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain for 5 weeks.

Patient has a history of stage IV transitional cell cancer with angiolymphatic invasion, treated with neo-adjuvant chemotherapy and radiation, radical cystectomy, ileal conduit, bilateral pelvic lymphadenectomy, and diverting sigmoid colostomy.

CT scan revealed new circumferential thickening and inflammatory stranding involving the ascending colon extending to the hepatic flexure, as well as the descending/transverse duodenal junction with adjacent inflammatory stranding.
CT scan also showed diffuse intra- and extra-hepatic biliary ductal and main pancreatic duct dilatation (double duct sign).
Upper endoscopy demonstrated duodenal stenosis with significant edema and congestion, traversable only with an ultrathin endoscope, confirming gastric outlet obstruction.
EGD biopsies of the duodenal lesion were non-diagnostic.

MRI of the abdomen confirmed the thickened descending duodenum and its abutment to the hepatic flexure, ruling out choledocholithiasis or pancreaticobiliary malignancy as the cause of the double duct sign.
Colonoscopy demonstrated a mass at the hepatic flexure.
Biopsies from the hepatic flexure mass confirmed invasive transitional cell cancer, linking the duodenal thickening and obstruction to metastatic disease.
